prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks into credit cycles and aggregate fluctuations

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a specific, tractable mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values link asset prices to investment and output, so that small, temporary shocks produce large and persistent fluctuations. The mechanism is the template for the collateral-constraint strand of macro-finance and is used in quantitative macro models, in work on housing and firm investment, and in post-2008 analysis of crises. The two-author attribution is unusually clean. A pair of laureates also avoids the crowded-credit problem that affects B001 and B047, and the idea has had nearly three decades to be extended and confirmed. After reading the openings, my ranking of B002 holds. The strongest challenge is that B001 has broader policy influence. That is a point about breadth of impact rather than about how cleanly the discovery can be credited, and I still weigh clean attribution heavily.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the Kiyotaki-Moore model is highly stylised, and direct empirical identification of the collateral channel mostly comes from later work by others. The ballot also credits Gertler and Gilchrist, whose financial-accelerator line is closely related, so reasonable members could argue that the discovery should be framed more broadly or that credit is split differently. The 2022 prize for banking and financial crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) may also reduce the committee's appetite for this theme. Finally, B001 has far wider support in the openings and a very large documented effect on central-bank practice. If the committee puts policy influence ahead of attribution clarity, B001 is the natural alternative.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first. He regards Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the most defensible three, notes that the post-2021 inflation episode tested the framework without overturning it, and ranks Kiyotaki-Moore fifth. He calls it highly stylised, with mixed empirical quantification, and says the financial-accelerator tradition sits on a parallel line.
responses.response: I agree that B001 has a first-order claim and that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are the cleanest trio inside it. I keep it as my alternative rather than my preferred part, because the exclusion of Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a larger attribution cost than anything in B002. I also accept that Kiyotaki-Moore is stylised. I read that as a strength of a foundational mechanism, which is why it spread through quantitative models, and I agree the empirical content came mostly from later calibrated and empirical work by others. On the parallel financial-accelerator line, we agree that Kiyotaki and Moore are the originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism, and that is the basis for the two-name credit.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and B002 eighth. He argues that the 2022 prize partly covers the financial-crisis theme, that Gertler's overlap with both B001 and B002 may matter, and that the Kiyotaki-Moore and Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist lines may be seen as competing.
responses.response: The overlap with 2022 is a real consideration, but I think it is smaller than suggested. The 2022 recognition concerned bank runs and the role of banks in the Great Depression. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values propagate and amplify shocks in production economies, which is a different discovery. I agree that credit would be messy if Gertler were added. That is why I propose only the two originators, and it also removes the Gertler overlap with B001. I do not think the possible competition with the financial-accelerator line is a reason to rank B002 as low as eighth, but I concede it is the main attribution risk.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B006 first and B002 second. He considers Kiyotaki-Moore the identifiable origin of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism and the cleanest attribution. He flags that Gertler's overlap with the New Keynesian candidate is a judgement call and that some of the empirical content rests on calibrated models.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and on the empirical caveat. The calibrated-model point is the reason I do not claim B002 as a strong case on empirical identification. Its strength is conceptual generality and its documented use in quantitative macro. Where we differ is on B006. I rank Persson and Tabellini fourth, because the identification of constitutional effects is weaker than the theory and the 2024 institutions prize makes the timing awkward. I would not exclude B006 on scientific grounds, and I keep it in mind as a serious fallback if B002 fails to gather support.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to frame the discovery as the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral-constraint mechanism alone or to add the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator strand, which would break the three-person limit or force a different laureate set.
How much weight the 2022 prize for banking and financial crises should carry against a distinct propagation mechanism.
Whether the limited direct empirical identification of collateral channels is acceptable for a foundational theory prize.
Whether B001's attribution can be resolved into a defensible three-person prize, or whether crowded credit is disqualifying. I have not changed my view that it is a hard problem.
I rely on the supplied openings and my own background knowledge. I have not independently verified citation or adoption figures.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent with the candidates on B002 from the supplied profile. The profile lists co-authorship with committee colleagues Krusell, Boppart and Friberg and IIES affiliation with Krusell and Boppart. None of them is a candidate on this ballot. My own research is in dynamic macroeconomics, public finance and climate economics, which is adjacent to several shortlisted fields but involves no named candidate.
